The title belongs to the Bugisu tribe, native to the mountain’s northwestern districts and who, during the final years of British colonialism, became entwined with agricultural politics through the formation of Uganda’s strongest coffee cooperative union. The Bugisu Cooperative Union was officially formed in 1954 after decades of struggle with British and European authority over control of the coffee on Mt. Elgon—considered Uganda’s best by far. During the first decades following formation, the union helped to mobilize and market the coffees from northwestern Mt. Elgon and was considered a strong source of unity for the Bugisu people as well as an economic empowerment engine for the greater native region. From the mid-50s to the mid-90s, as production increased, “Bugisu” became synonymous with top quality coffee from Uganda. Since the wane of cooperative unions nationwide during the 1990s, “Bugisu” has remained a prideful mark of smallholder coffee from the western slope of Mt. Elgon. Kawacom, one of Uganda’s top exporters, invests heavily in the potential of this area and keeps the Bugisu history alive in their profiles. Sebastian Mejia comes from a coffee-growing family with deep roots in conventional coffee production. But after years of low coffee prices, his family made the difficult decision to sell their farms and shift into dairy cattle production. Financial challenges eventually led them to sell that land and livestock as well, opening the door to a new beginning in La Peña, Santa Barbara.

There, Sebastian and his family invested in what is now Finca Gonzalo, a 2.8-hectare farm sitting at 1,530 meters above sea level. Drawing on the experience of relatives and neighboring producers who had already moved into specialty coffee, Sebastian began focusing on higher-quality production with a long-term vision for the farm.

Today, Parainema is the primary variety grown at Finca Gonzalo, with young Geisha plants gradually being introduced. About half of the farm is maintained under controlled shade, and Sebastian also grows avocados, bananas, and blackberries alongside the coffee. He uses poultry manure and coffee pulp as part of his fertilization program, supplementing with locally blended inputs based on the needs of the area.

Like many producers in the region, Sebastian faces ongoing challenges on the farm. Labor is increasingly difficult to find as many younger people leave the area for opportunities in the United States. Coffee rust and other diseases remain a constant concern, and poor road conditions make accessing the property especially difficult.

Despite those challenges, Sebastian is focused on continuing to build Finca Gonzalo for the future. His plans include constructing a wet mill, improving road access to the farm, building a home on the property, purchasing additional land for coffee production, and developing a reliable water source for the farm.

What makes Sebastian’s story especially compelling is that coffee represents a return for his family. After stepping away from coffee once before, they’ve come back to it with a renewed focus on quality, sustainability, and building something that can continue to grow for years to come. We look forward to building upon this relationship for many years ahead.

ASOPCE (Association of Specialty Coffee Producers of Huehuetenango) is a smallholder farmers’ association working across the remote mountain communities of Huehuetenango. Founded in 2015, the association was created to unify producers from Huehuetenango and neighboring areas of San Marcos and to place their coffees in international markets at fair prices. Today, ASOPCE represents approximately 450 smallholder producers, most farming small plots averaging 1.5 hectares at elevations between 1,400 and 2,050 MASL. Each producer family manages their own wet milling and patio drying, following established quality standards, with parchment stored at ASOPCE’s central bodega prior to export. The cooperative provides technical assistance, commercialization, and access to credit, supporting improved crop performance and long-term livelihoods. Women represent approximately 30% of ASOPCE’s membership and manage or own their own production units. This coffee was grown using organic practices by certified organic producers at origin.

Coffees in Ethiopia are typically grown on very small plots of land by farmers who also grow other crops. The majority of smallholders will deliver their coffee in cherry to a nearby washing station or central processing unit, where their coffee will be sorted, weighed, and paid for or given a receipt. The washing stations serve as many as several hundred to sometimes a thousand or more producers, who deliver cherry throughout the harvest season: The blending of these cherries into day lots makes it virtually impossible under normal circumstances to know precisely whose coffee winds up in which bags on what day, making traceability to the producer difficult.
